questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: compute flux as B times A times the cosine of the angle
questions.stem: A square loop of area 0.04 m^2 sits in a 0.5 T uniform field. When the loop lies flat in the field the flux is 0.02 Wb, and when it is tipped upright the flux is 0 Wb. Which angle did the loop move through, measured between the field and the loop's area vector?

options.text: 90 degrees, because the area vector went from parallel to the field to perpendicular to it
45 degrees, because the flux fell to half rather than to zero
options.misconception: believes a halving of flux means a 45 degree turn

options.text: 180 degrees, because the loop must fully reverse to lose all flux
options.misconception: confuses losing flux with reversing the area vector

options.text: 0 degrees, because flux depends only on the field strength
options.misconception: ignores the angle term in the flux formula

questions.explanation: Flux is Phi = B times A times cos(theta), where theta is measured from the field to the loop's area vector. A flat loop in the field has its area vector perpendicular to B, so theta is 0 and flux is largest at 0.02 Wb. Tipping it upright points the area vector along the field, so theta is 90 degrees and cos(theta) is 0, which is why the flux falls to exactly 0 Wb.
questions.hint: Ask what angle makes the cosine term equal to zero.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: apply the average emf as N times the change in flux per second
questions.stem: A single loop of area 0.05 m^2 sits in a field that drops uniformly from 0.8 T to 0.3 T over 0.25 s while the loop stays flat. What is the average induced emf in volts? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The flux change is the area times the change in field, since the loop does not move: 0.8 minus 0.3 gives 0.5 T, and 0.5 times 0.05 is 0.025 Wb. Dividing that change by the 0.25 s gives an emf of 0.025 / 0.25 = 0.1 V. The tempting 100 V answer comes from multiplying by the elapsed time instead of dividing by it.
questions.hint: Flux change is the area times the change in field, not the area times the field itself.

questions.explanation: Faraday's law gives emf = N times the rate of change of flux, so 150 turns times 0.08 Wb per second is 12 V. A student who forgets the N gets 0.08 V, and one who treats flux linkage as already including the turns gets the same tiny answer.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: state that the induced current opposes the change that produced it
questions.stem: A bar magnet is pushed toward a closed conducting loop. Which statement correctly describes the current that appears in the loop as the magnet approaches?

options.text: A current flows that makes the loop's near face act like a north pole, repelling the approaching magnet
A current flows that makes the loop's near face act like a south pole, attracting the approaching magnet
options.misconception: believes the induced current reinforces the change instead of opposing it

options.text: No current flows, because the magnet has not yet touched the loop
options.misconception: thinks induction requires physical contact with the source

options.text: A current flows only once the magnet actually enters the loop's opening
options.misconception: believes the field must be enclosed to induce anything

questions.explanation: Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change in flux. As the north pole approaches, the flux through the loop grows, so the induced current creates its own field pointing back at the magnet, which requires a north pole facing the magnet and therefore a repulsive force. A south-pole answer would attract the magnet and make the approach faster, which would violate conservation of energy.
questions.hint: Ask whether attraction or repulsion keeps the energy supply honest.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose of the negative sign in Faraday's law
questions.stem: Faraday's law is written emf = -N times d(Phi)/dt. A student asks what the minus sign contributes. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: It encodes Lenz's law, so the induced effect always opposes the change that created it
It corrects for the fact that the field strength is usually given as a negative number
options.misconception: believes fields are routinely negative and the sign repairs that

options.text: It shows that the induced emf is always smaller than the original field, with no limit
options.misconception: reads the sign as a guaranteed magnitude reduction

options.text: It appears because flux and time are both measured in negative units in the SI system
options.misconception: invents negative units for flux and time

questions.explanation: The minus sign is not bookkeeping; it is Lenz's law written into the formula. Without it, a growing flux would predict an induced effect that reinforces the growth, which would let perpetual motion extract energy from nothing. The sign guarantees the induced current always fights the change.
questions.hint: Ask what a reinforcing induced current would let you build.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: apply the motional emf relation for a rod moving in a magnetic field
questions.stem: A 2 m long conducting rod slides along rails at 5 m/s in a 0.3 T field, with its length perpendicular to both the field and its velocity. What emf appears between its ends in volts? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The motional emf is emf = B times L times v, so 0.3 T times 2 m times 5 m/s is 3 V. A student who multiplies the two lengths together, or who forgets one of the three factors, lands on a very different number; 6 V comes from doubling a single factor by mistake.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: identify when a moving conductor develops an emf
questions.stem: A copper rod moves through a uniform 0.5 T field. In which case does a voltage develop between the rod's ends?

options.text: When the rod moves perpendicular to the field, so the charge carriers are pushed along the rod
When the rod moves parallel to the field, since parallel motion pushes harder
options.misconception: believes parallel motion gives a stronger push than perpendicular

options.text: When the rod rotates in place about its center, since rotation is the same as translation
options.misconception: confuses rotation of the rod with translation through the field

options.text: Never, because a voltage needs a battery to supply the charge separation
options.misconception: believes induced charge separation must be battery-driven

questions.explanation: The magnetic force on a charge is q times v cross B, which vanishes when the velocity is parallel to the field because the cross product is then zero. Only motion with a component perpendicular to the field pushes positive and negative carriers apart along the rod, producing a voltage.
questions.hint: Evaluate the cross product of velocity with field for each case.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain how an inductor resists a change in its own current
questions.stem: A switch closes and current starts to build in a large solenoid. Why does the circuit briefly resist the current at the instant the switch closes?

options.text: The growing current creates its own changing flux, which induces a back emf that opposes the growth
The wire heats up on contact and the heating effect opposes the current
options.misconception: substitutes thermal resistance for inductive back emf

options.text: The battery spends its first moments charging the wire's internal capacitance
options.misconception: invokes capacitance where self inductance is the relevant effect

options.text: The switch contacts start open and the gap blocks current until they arc closed
options.misconception: attributes the delay to the switch hardware rather than the coil

Lenz's law fixes its direction: it opposes the rise, which is why a large inductor behaves like an added resistance at switch-on and then settles to a steady current once the flux stops changing.

questions.learningObjective: compute the peak emf of a rotating coil
questions.stem: A 200 turn coil of area 0.01 m^2 rotates at 10 revolutions per second in a 0.3 T field. What is the peak induced emf in volts? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The peak emf of a rotating coil is N times B times A times omega, where omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi times 10, which is about 62.83 rad/s. Multiplying gives 200 times 0.3 times 0.01 times 62.83 = 37.7 V. Forgetting the factor of two pi and using f directly gives only 6 V.
questions.hint: Convert revolutions per second to radians per second before using the formula.

questions.learningObjective: recognize that only a change in flux induces an emf
questions.stem: A loop sits motionless in a strong, steady magnetic field. What emf, if any, appears across the loop's terminals, and why?

options.text: No emf, because the flux through the loop is large but not changing over time
A large emf, because a large flux always produces a large induced voltage
options.misconception: confuses flux itself with its rate of change

options.text: No emf, because the loop is closed and a closed loop short-circuits any voltage
options.misconception: invents a short-circuit rule for induced emf

options.text: A small emf, because the field always leaks a little energy into any conductor
options.misconception: believes a static field leaks into nearby conductors

questions.explanation: Faraday's law depends on d(Phi)/dt, not on Phi itself. A loop resting in an unchanging field has zero rate of flux change no matter how strong the field is, so no emf appears. Induction requires motion, a changing field, or a changing orientation, and it is the change that supplies the energy.

It rises, because tilting the loop lets more field pass through the opening
options.misconception: believes tilting always increases the captured area

options.text: It stays the same, because flux depends only on the loop's total area
options.misconception: ignores the projection factor entirely

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: isolate which quantity must change for induction to occur
questions.stem: A coil's induced emf has dropped to zero. Which change, if any, would restore a nonzero emf?

options.text: Rotating the coil steadily so that the angle between its area vector and the field keeps changing
Holding the coil perfectly still while keeping the field magnitude constant
options.misconception: believes a steady field with a still coil still induces

options.text: Warming the coil until its resistance drops to nearly zero
options.misconception: confuses resistance change with flux change

options.text: Replacing the coil with an identical one wound from thicker wire
options.misconception: believes wire thickness is what sets the induced emf

questions.explanation: A nonzero emf requires a nonzero rate of change of flux, and flux is B times A times cos(theta). A still coil in a steady field has zero rate of change, and neither resistance nor wire thickness enters Faraday's law.

questions.learningObjective: apply the solenoid inductance relation
questions.stem: An air-core solenoid has 500 turns per meter, a cross-sectional area of 1e-4 m^2, and a length of 0.5 m. Using mu_0 = 1.26e-6 H/m, what is its inductance in microhenries? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The solenoid relation is L = mu_0 times n squared times A times length, so 1.26e-6 times 500 squared gives 0.315, and multiplying by 1e-4 and 0.5 gives 1.575e-5 H, which is 15.75 microhenries. Using n instead of n squared yields an inductance a million times too small.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: use Lenz's law to set the direction of an induced current
questions.stem: A loop is pulled out of a region of uniform field so that its flux through the field drops. Which direction does the induced current run as seen from the side where the loop is being pulled away?

options.text: A current flows that creates a field pointing back into the field region, opposing the loss
A current flows that reinforces the outward field, speeding the loop's exit
options.misconception: believes the induced current pushes the loop out faster

options.text: No current flows, because the loop has already left the field region
options.misconception: believes leaving the field stops induction immediately

options.text: A current flows that alternates direction as the loop moves, since the emf is negative
options.misconception: reads a negative emf as a sign that the current reverses

questions.explanation: As the loop leaves, the inward flux decreases, so Lenz's law requires the induced current to oppose that decrease by creating its own inward field. That means the current circulates in the same sense as it would for a shrinking inward flux, and the force on the loop opposes the withdrawal, which is why pulling a loop out of a field costs mechanical work.
questions.hint: Ask which way the induced field must point to oppose a loss of flux.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain why Lenz's law is required by energy conservation
questions.stem: A student claims they could build a generator that produces more electrical energy than the mechanical work used to spin the coil, because the coil also pushes back on the magnets. Explain in your own words why that is impossible.

answer.exemplar: The push-back is not extra energy, it is energy already spent. Lenz's law forces the induced current to oppose the change in flux, so the coil always resists the motion that creates it. The mechanical work you put in against that resistance appears as the electrical energy you collect, so the two can at best balance and never produce a surplus.

questions.explanation: This item has no single correct option; a full-credit response must state that the induced current opposes the change by Lenz's law, connect that opposition to a retarding mechanical force, and conclude that the electrical energy out can at most equal the work in. A response that claims the opposition force is an extra output, or that ignores the opposition entirely, misses the conservation argument.
questions.hint: Follow the energy: what work does the resisting force cost the person turning the coil?

questions.learningObjective: distinguish the roles of the loop area and the rod length

The loop width w, because the emf comes from the rails being wider
options.misconception: attributes the emf to the stationary rail separation

options.text: The loop area L times w, because the emf must use the full enclosed area
options.misconception: substitutes the loop area for the moving conductor length

options.text: The product L times w, which is the area and therefore always the correct factor
options.misconception: doubles up on the area after already using the length

The loop width w only sets how fast the enclosed flux changes, because the area swept per unit time is L times v, not w times v. Substituting the area for the length therefore double-counts one factor of L.

It stays the same, because the flux through the coil is unchanged by rewinding

options.text: It quadruples, because the turns multiply the area as well as the flux

questions.learningObjective: identify the factors that set a generator's output frequency
questions.stem: A generator's coil is turned at 20 revolutions per second. How many times per second does the induced emf reach its peak magnitude in one direction?

40 times per second, because each revolution produces two peaks of opposite sign
options.misconception: counts peak magnitude per half turn as if it were a separate peak

options.text: 10 times per second, because only one peak per revolution has the larger value
options.misconception: counts only the positive half of the cycle

options.text: 20 times per second with a zero average, so the emf carries no power at all
options.misconception: confuses zero average with zero useful power

The magnitude therefore returns to its peak value once per revolution, giving 20 peaks per second at 20 revolutions per second. questions.hint: Distinguish peaks of the magnitude from sign changes within one cycle.

answer.exemplar: A static field gives a constant flux, and the induced emf depends on how fast that flux changes, not on how large it is. Least of all

questions.explanation: The ordering runs from the fastest, largest rate of flux change to the slowest. A field collapsing over milliseconds, a loop yanked out of a field, a coil rotating steadily, and finally a loop sitting still in a constant field produce progressively smaller rates of change, with the last case producing exactly zero.
questions.hint: Rank them by how fast the flux through the loop is changing.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of a large inductance on a circuit's time response
questions.stem: A very large inductor is placed in series with a lamp and a battery, and the switch is closed. What does the student observe, and why?

options.text: The lamp glows a moment later, because the inductor's back emf holds the current down while it builds
The lamp glows immediately and dimmer forever, because the inductor steals a fixed share of current
options.misconception: believes inductance behaves like a fixed resistance divider

options.text: The lamp never glows, because an inductor blocks current permanently once switched in
options.misconception: treats inductance as a permanent block rather than a transient opposition

options.text: The lamp glows only after the inductor is fully saturated and stops resisting
options.misconception: invokes saturation to explain a transient that needs no saturation

questions.explanation: A large inductance makes the current build slowly because the back emf L times dI/dt opposes any change in current. That delay is transient: once the current settles and dI/dt falls to zero, the back emf vanishes, the inductor behaves like a plain wire, and the lamp reaches full brightness.
questions.hint: The back emf depends on the rate of change, so ask what happens when the rate falls to zero.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: identify all three conditions required for motional emf
questions.stem: Which set of conditions must all hold for a moving conductor to develop an emf across its ends?

options.text: A magnetic field is present, the conductor moves, and the velocity has a component perpendicular to the field
A magnetic field is present, the conductor is charged, and the circuit is closed
options.misconception: substitutes net charge and a closed loop for perpendicular motion

options.text: A magnetic field is present, the conductor is at rest, and the circuit is open
options.misconception: claims a resting conductor develops an emf from field alone

options.text: A magnetic field is present, the conductor moves parallel to it, and the loop stays closed
options.misconception: believes parallel motion still separates charges along the rod

questions.explanation: The magnetic force on a charge is proportional to v cross B, so a field alone does nothing, motion alone does nothing, and motion parallel to the field gives a zero cross product. All three conditions, including a perpendicular velocity component, must hold together, which is why the emf appears only when the geometry actually changes the flux.
questions.hint: Evaluate the cross product of velocity with field for each candidate set.
